passages.t: The LORD's case against the land
passages.happening:
‘Hear the word of the LORD, O children of Israel, for the LORD has a case against the people of the land’ (verse 1). The charge is that there is no truth, no loving devotion and no knowledge of God in the land.

Instead, ‘Cursing and lying, murder and stealing, and adultery are rampant; one act of bloodshed follows another’ (verse 2). So the land mourns. Its people waste away, and with them the animals, the birds and even the fish of the sea (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
With chapter 4 the book moves from Hosea's household to his public preaching. Chapters 4 to 14 are a collection of oracles, most of them undated, spoken to the northern kingdom in its last decades. This chapter works like an opening statement in court, and the rest of the book develops its charges. The chapter fits the years around the end of Jeroboam II's reign, when Israel was still wealthy but had lost its way.

The word for case, riv, is a word for a lawsuit. The prophets often pictured God bringing a legal complaint against Israel for breaking the covenant. God is both the wronged party and the judge.

The three missing things are the marks of a faithful covenant partner. Truth is faithfulness. Loving devotion is hesed, loyal covenant love. Knowledge of God, in Hosea, is not information about him but knowing him, owning him as God and living by his teaching. The crimes of verse 2 echo the Ten Commandments, the heart of the covenant. When a people stops knowing God, the commandments go, and even the land suffers.
passages.later: Other prophets also called Israel into court: ‘Listen, O heavens, and give ear, O earth’ (Isaiah 1:2), and Micah summons the mountains to hear the LORD's case (Micah 6:1-2). The crimes of verse 2 follow the commandments given at Sinai (Exodus 20:13-16).
passages.asks: Hosea traces cursing, lying and violence back to one root: no knowledge of God. Ask what difference knowing God, and not only knowing about him, makes in the way a person treats others. And ask what your own life would say in a court like this one.

passages.happening:
The LORD turns on the priests. Priest and prophet stumble together (verses 4-5). ‘My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you as My priests. Since you have forgotten the law of your God, I will also forget your children’ (verse 6).

The more the priests multiplied, the more they sinned. They exchanged their Glory for disgrace, and they feed on the people's sins (verses 7-8). ‘And it shall be like people, like priest’ (verse 9). Both will be punished. They will eat and not be satisfied, because they have stopped obeying the LORD (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Israel's priests served at royal shrines such as Bethel and Gilgal, not at the temple in Jerusalem. That went back to Jeroboam I, who appointed priests of his own choosing and set up the golden calves. A priest's task was not only to offer sacrifices but to teach the law. When the priests stopped teaching, the knowledge of God failed with them.

The words about a people destroyed for lack of knowledge are often quoted as if they were about education in general. Here it is about a people who no longer know their God, because those who should have taught them have forgotten him. Verse 8 may mean that the priests profited from the people's sin offerings, so the more the people sinned, the more the priests ate.

Notice the way the punishment matches the sin. Because the priests forgot God's law, God will forget their children. Like people, like priest: the leaders and the people share the same guilt and will share the same judgment. The Hebrew of verse 4 is hard, and translations vary.
passages.later: The law gave the priests the work of teaching (Leviticus 10:11; Deuteronomy 33:10), and the last of the prophets says, ‘For the lips of a priest should preserve knowledge’ (Malachi 2:7). In Hosea's own day, Amos clashed with Amaziah, the priest of Bethel (Amos 7:10-13).
passages.asks: The priests who should have taught God's ways had forgotten them, and the people paid for it. Ask who has taught you, and what you owe them. And if you teach or lead anyone, ask whether you know God yourself, or only the work of religion.

passages.t: A spirit of prostitution at the shrines
passages.happening:
Promiscuity and wine take away understanding (verse 11). The people consult wooden idols and divining rods, because ‘a spirit of prostitution leads them astray’ (verse 12). They sacrifice on the hilltops under oak, poplar and terebinth, ‘because their shade is pleasant’ (verse 13), and their daughters and daughters-in-law turn to prostitution and adultery.

Yet God will not punish the daughters, because the men themselves go off with prostitutes and offer sacrifices with shrine prostitutes (verse 14). Judah must not follow: do not go to Gilgal or up to Beth-aven (verse 15). ‘For Israel is as obstinate as a stubborn heifer’ (verse 16). Ephraim is joined to idols. The whirlwind has wrapped them in its wings, and their sacrifices will bring them shame (verses 17-19).
passages.hearers:
Hosea describes worship at open-air shrines on hilltops and under shady trees, places long tied to fertility religion. Consulting wooden idols and divining rods was an old way of seeking omens.

The BSB calls some of the women at the shrines shrine prostitutes. The Hebrew word means a consecrated woman, from the word for holy: what was set apart for a god has been turned to immorality. Older scholarship widely assumed that Canaanite religion used ritual sex to make the fields fertile. Many scholars now doubt that sacred prostitution was as common as once thought, and the word may describe women attached to shrines whose role is not fully understood. What Hosea condemns is plain: sexual immorality mixed with worship, led by the men of Israel.

Gilgal, near Jericho, was an old holy place where Israel camped after crossing the Jordan and where Saul was made king. Beth-aven, house of wickedness, is Hosea's mocking name for Bethel, house of God, the chief royal shrine of the north. A stubborn heifer will not be led, and a shepherd cannot lead it to good pasture.
passages.later: Gilgal was where Israel camped after crossing the Jordan (Joshua 4:19-20) and where Saul was made king (1 Samuel 11:14-15). The law had forbidden worship under every green tree on the hills (Deuteronomy 12:2), and it forbade the role of a consecrated woman in Israel (Deuteronomy 23:17).
passages.hard:
Why does God say he will not punish the daughters who commit adultery?

Verse 14 is surprising in a culture that often blamed women first. God declines to punish the daughters and daughters-in-law, and he gives the reason: the men themselves go off with prostitutes and sacrifice with them at the shrines. This does not mean that the women's sin does not matter. It means that the men, the heads of households and the worshipers who set the example, bear the greater guilt. The double standard that punished women and excused men is turned around.

Interpreters differ on the setting. Some think the verse refers to sexual rites at the shrines, in which young women took part under the direction of the men and the priests. Others, doubting that such rites were common, read it as a picture of a general collapse of sexual morality in a society whose worship had lost its center. Either way, the chapter lays the responsibility on those with power and knowledge. Those who teach and lead are judged more strictly.
passages.asks: The people worshiped where the shade was pleasant. Ask whether you choose your worship for comfort or for God. And verse 14 lays the heavier blame on the men who led. Ask where you have power over others, and how you are using it.
